paragraphs: Micro-aerated fermentation enhances acetate production from high-rate activated sludge to supply carbon source for heterotrophic denitratation
Yexuan Wena,b, Haixin Jianga,b, Ruibo Qiana,b, Shiting Liuc, Xianchun Tanga,b, Weiping Huanga,b, Hongbin Chena,b,*
a State Key Laboratory of Pollution Control and Resource Reuse, College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
b National Engineering Research Center for Urban Pollution Control, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
c Sichuan Environmental Protection Industry Group Company Limited, Chengdu 610046, China
*Corresponding author: Hongbin Chen, Professor, College of Environment Science and Engineering, Tongji University, Email: bhctxc@tongji.edu.cn, Tel: 0086-21-65984569; FAX: 0086-21-65983602.

For 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, 40 mL fresh raw CEHRAS and fermented sludge from MaSBR and AnSBR were collected with three parallel samples for each. The samples were centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, after which the supernatant was removed, leaving only the biomass pellet to be stored at -80 ℃ until DNA extraction. The DNA was extracted using the FastDNA® SPIN kit for soil (MP Biomedicals, Santa Ana, CA, USA) according to manufacturer’s instructions.

The hypervariable region V3-V4 of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene were amplified with primer pairs 338F (5'-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3') and 806R (5'-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3') by an ABI GeneAmp® 9700 PCR thermocycler (ABI, CA, USA). The PCR amplification of 16S rRNA gene was performed as follows: initial denaturation at 95 ℃ for 3 min, followed by 27 cycles of denaturing at 95 ℃ for 30 s, annealing at 55 ℃ for 30 s and extension at 72 ℃ for 45 s, and single extension at 72 ℃ for 10 min, and end at 4 ℃. The PCR mixtures contain 5 × TransStart FastPfu buffer 4 μL, 2.5 mM dNTPs 2 μL, forward primer (5 μM) 0.8 μL, reverse primer (5 μM) 0.8 μL, TransStart FastPfu DNA Polymerase 0.4 μL, template DNA 10 ng, and finally ddH2O up to 20 μL. PCR reactions were performed in triplicate. The PCR product was extracted from 2% agarose gel and purified using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen Biosciences, Union City, CA, USA) according to manufacturer’s instructions and quantified using Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega, USA). Amplicons were subjected to paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform using PE300 chemical at Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The raw reads were deposited into the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database (Accession Number: PRJNA819234).

After demultiplexing, the resulting sequences were merged with Flash (version 1.2.11) [1] and quality filtered with Fastp (0.19.6) [2]. Then the high-quality sequences were de-noised using DADA2 [3] plugin in the Qiime2 [4] (version 1.9.1) pipeline with recommended parameters, which obtains single nucleotide resolution based on error profiles within samples. DADA2 denoised sequences are usually called amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). Taxonomic assignment of ASVs was performed using the Naive bayes consensus taxonomy classifier implemented in Qiime2 and the SILVA 16S rRNA database (version 138). Analyses of the 16S rRNA microbiome sequencing data was performed using the free online platform of Majorbio Cloud Platform (cloud.majorbio.com).

Volatile solids (VSS), total nitrogen (TN), NH4-N, NO3-N, NO2-N, and PO4-P were determined by the standard methods [5]. A HACH test kit TNT 822 was used to test COD. Protein and L-glutamate was measured by using the Modified BCA Kit (Sangon, China) and Micro Amino Acid Content Assay Kit (Solaribio, China), respectively. Polysaccharide and dextran were both measured by the phenol sulfuric acid method, with glucose and dextran as standards, respectively. An EEM fluorescence spectrometer (Aqualog, HORIBA, France) was used to analyze the changes of dissolved organic matter in sludge. The gas composition (i.e., methane) was analyzed by gas chromatography (GC6890, Agilent, USA) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector. The VFAs were quantified by using a gas chromatography (GC6890, Agilent, USA) according to the following procedure, the column operating profiles were 55 ℃ for 1 min, then 30 ℃/min to 110 ℃, then hold for 1 min, finally 10 ℃/min to 200 ℃ and 30 ℃/min to 220 ℃.
Results of the DSTSD model fitting batch experimental data

The batch denitrification experimental data with synthetic and real fermentate as carbon source and the corresponding model simulations are shown in Fig. 8. While the objective function is the errors’ sum of all synthetic fermentate experimental data, the estimated parameter values are listed as Value Set 1 in Table S3. Although the DSTSD model fitted well the synthetic fermentate experimental data using parameter values of Set 1, the experimental data of real fermentate cannot be fitted well. There are three possible reasons as follows. First, the real fermentate contains fermentable components, which can be hydrolyzed to VFA during the denitrification. Second, the real fermentate contains other VFA-like components, which can be taken up directly and stored in the form of intracellular storage product (XSTO). Third, the real fermentate contains acceleration or inhibition factors to biological processes. For the first principle, hydrolysis process of the fermentable components should be added into the DSTSD model. However, in this case, the model simulation showed a tendency that the SAC decreased firstly and then increased (not shown in this study), which was inconsistent with the observed data. For the second and third principles, regulating the sensitive parameters rather than increasing model processes can realize good fitting results to the experimental data. The regulated parameter values are listed as Value Set 2 in Table S3. The final fitting results are exhibited in Fig. 8(k).
Calculations of carbon source requirement for nitrate and nitrite reduction

This approach requires the lower carbon source amount for the reduction of nitrate to dinitrogen: Nitrate is firstly reduced to nitrite with the extracellular carbon source, and then reduced to dinitrogen with the internal storage products (XSTO) rather than completely relying on the extracellular carbon source. Moreover, the yields of XSTO s from acetate and non-acetate are the same (YSTO). Hence, we can use processes 1 and 6 (Table S2) to figure out the minimal carbon source requirement of the reduction of nitrate to dinitrogen. As we can see from the process 1 row in Table S2, one unit of acetate will produce YSTO units of XSTO and reduce (1 - YSTO)/(16/14) units of nitrate. From the process 6 row, we can know one unit of XSTO can be utilized to reduce (1 - YANG)/(24/14) units of nitrite. Therefore, the unit amounts of nitrate that can be reduced to dinitrogen with one unit of acetate is:
When YSTO = 0.80 and YANG = 0.54, the value is 4.66 g COD/g N.

The same with the reduction of nitrate to dinitrogen, processes 1 and 5 or processes 2 and 5 in Table S2 can be used to calculate the minimal carbon source requirement of the reduction of nitrate to nitrite. Here, we use processes 1 and 5. The minimal carbon source requirement is:
The first and second terms in the denominator are related to process 1 and 5, respectively. When YSTO = 0.80 and YANG = 0.54, this value is 2.01 g COD/g N.
